source: Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb, Demszky (2024, v3 2026) Tutor CoPilot
finding: RCT of an LLM that gives live expert-style scaffolds to human tutors. Students of treated tutors passed exit tickets more often.
numbers: 900 tutors randomised (450/450); 783 tutored in study (388 treated, 395 control); about 7 weeks in 2024. Exit-ticket pass 62% to 66% (+4 pp, p<.01, intent-to-treat). Treatment-on-treated +14 pp. About $20 per tutor per year.
limits: Randomised by tutor, not student; outcome is session exit tickets, not end-of-year scores. Single provider and district.
agent_relevance: Scaffolding a weaker helper with expert-thinking prompts works at small cost. Supports a lesson library that prompts the agent, not one that replaces its reasoning.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Tutor CoPilot, heterogeneity
finding: Gains were largest for weaker tutors. Scaffold narrows the gap between novices and experts, and fades in value as skill rises.
numbers: Lower-rated tutors: 56% to 65% (+9 pp). Less experienced tutors: 61% to 68% (+7 pp). Treated low-rated tutors matched control high-rated tutors.
limits: Effect shrinks with tutor quality, a pattern like the expertise reversal effect. Heterogeneity analysis is secondary.
agent_relevance: A scaffold should be strongest for weak or unfamiliar problem types and fade for strong ones (do not over-prompt a competent state).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Tutor CoPilot, language analysis
finding: Treated tutors used more probing questions and less generic praise, over 350,000 messages. Behaviour moved toward scaffolding, away from telling.
numbers: More than 350,000 messages analysed; log-odds shifts reported per strategy (Tables 15-19).
limits: Language proxies for quality; link to learning is not tested directly.
agent_relevance: Questions that elicit the learner's own step are the observable mark of a good scaffold; the agent can log this.

source: Kestin, Miller, Klales, Milbourne, Ponti (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning
finding: Harvard physics RCT (crossover). A purpose-built AI tutor with step-by-step scaffolding beat in-class active learning on post-test gains.
numbers: Course N = 233, analysed N = 194; median post-score 4.5 (AI, N=142) vs 3.5 (active learning, N=174); pre-test median 2.75. Median gain more than double. Effect size 0.63 by linear regression; 0.73 to 1.3 SD by quantile regression. p<1e-8. Median AI time on task 49 minutes; time on task did not correlate with post-score.
limits: One course, one topic pair, short test; ceiling effect; active-learning arm was one lesson, not the whole method. Tutor was prompted with instructor-written solutions.
agent_relevance: Large gains came when the AI was pre-loaded with correct worked solutions and told to scaffold stepwise. Supports verified lessons as scaffold content.

source: Bastani, Bastani, Sungu, Ge, Kabakci, Mariman (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning
finding: Unguarded GPT-4 helped practice scores but hurt later unaided exam scores. A hint-only tutor with teacher-written solutions removed the harm.
numbers: About 1,000 Turkish high-school students, about 50 classes, four 90-minute sessions. Practice: GPT Base +48%, GPT Tutor +127% vs control (control mean 0.28). Exam without access: GPT Base -17% (significant); GPT Tutor about 0, no gain.
limits: One school, one subject, Fall 2023 (GPT-4). Even the guarded tutor produced no learning gain on the exam. Read via Europe PMC full text.
agent_relevance: Key warning: help that carries the performance can block learning. Scaffold must fade or withhold answers; performance with the scaffold is not evidence of internalised skill.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) mechanism: wrong model answers
finding: Base GPT-4 was often wrong on the practice items, and students copied. Teacher-supplied solutions and common-mistake notes in the prompt fixed this.
numbers: GPT Base correct only 51% of the time: 42% logical errors, 8% arithmetic errors. Students did not perceive any reduction in their own learning.
limits: Error rate is for GPT-4 on these Turkish textbook items in 2023; stronger models would differ.
agent_relevance: A scaffold made from unverified model output can be wrong half the time. Lessons stored for later use need verification before they are reused.

source: Nickow, Oreopoulos, Quan (2020) Impressive Impacts of Tutoring on PreK-12 Learning (NBER w27476)
finding: Meta-analysis of randomised tutoring trials. Tutoring gives large, consistent gains.
numbers: Pooled effect 0.37 SD. Stronger for teacher and paraprofessional tutors than non-professional or parent tutors; larger in earlier grades; in-school more than after-school. Reading and maths about equal overall.
limits: Only the abstract page was read here, so counts of studies are not recorded. Human tutoring, not LLMs. Tutoring bundles scaffolding with time and attention.
agent_relevance: Sets a human benchmark of about 0.4 SD for a good tutor; an LLM scaffold claim should be compared to this scale.

source: Lazonder & Harmsen (2016) Meta-analysis of inquiry-based learning: effects of guidance (via TUM summary)
finding: Guidance in inquiry learning helps. Types of guidance mostly did not differ from each other in effect.
numbers: 72 studies 1993-2013, learners aged 5 to 22 in STEM. Learning activities d=0.66 (20 studies), performance success d=0.71 (17 studies), learning outcomes d=0.50 (60 studies).
limits: Read a German summary, not the full article. Effects were larger for process than for final learning. Mostly simulation-based inquiry.
agent_relevance: Some guidance beats none, but the exact form matters less than its presence. A simple scaffold may be enough; do not over-engineer types.

source: Kim, Belland, Walker (2018) Effectiveness of computer-based scaffolding in problem-centered instruction (Bayesian meta-analysis)
finding: Bayesian meta-analysis of computer scaffolds in STEM problem-based learning. Overall effect small to moderate, varying by context.
numbers: Overall g = 0.385 on cognitive outcomes; six moderators with 24 subcategories.
limits: Only the abstract page was read. Study count not stated there. Prior choice affects estimates.
agent_relevance: A realistic prior for a built-in scaffold is g near 0.4, not 1.0.

source: Belland, Walker, Kim, Lefler (2017) Synthesizing results from computer-based scaffolding in STEM (Rev. Educ. Res.)
finding: Large meta-analysis: computer scaffolds help across scaffold types, contexts and assessment levels.
numbers: 144 experimental studies, 333 outcomes, mean g = 0.46 (from a search summary of the abstract, not the paper).
limits: Not opened; page blocked. Largest effects at the principles level of assessment and among adults, per that summary.
agent_relevance: Same scale as other scaffold meta-analyses (0.4 to 0.5).

source: VanLehn (2011) The relative effectiveness of human tutoring, intelligent tutoring systems, and other tutoring systems
finding: Review of 80+ studies. The size of the unit of interaction matters more than whether a human or a machine tutors.
numbers: From memory: human tutoring d=0.79; step-based ITS d=0.76; substep-based d=0.40; answer-based d=0.31, all vs no tutoring. Bloom's 2 sigma judged an overestimate.
limits: Not opened this session; page returned 403. Numbers from memory and should be checked.
agent_relevance: Step-level feedback (the granularity of a state in our schema) captures nearly all the human-tutor benefit; answer-only feedback does little.

source: Ma, Adesope, Nesbit, Liu (2014) Intelligent tutoring systems and learning outcomes: a meta-analysis
finding: ITS beat large-group instruction and textbook work, and were about equal to human tutors.
numbers: From memory: 107 effect sizes; g=0.41 overall vs non-ITS; ITS vs human tutors g=-0.11, not significant.
limits: Not opened this session. Numbers from memory.
agent_relevance: Machine scaffolding can reach human-tutor level when the domain is well modelled.

source: Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich, Tenenbaum (2011) Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
finding: Unassisted discovery is worse than direct teaching, but guided (enhanced) discovery with feedback, worked examples or scaffolds is better.
numbers: From memory: unassisted discovery vs other instruction d about -0.38; enhanced discovery d about +0.30. 164 studies.
limits: Not opened; numbers from memory.
agent_relevance: Settles the Kirschner-Sweller-Clark vs Hmelo-Silver dispute in favour of guided exploration: free self-exploration without scaffold underperforms.

source: Wood, Bruner, Ross (1976) The role of tutoring in problem solving
finding: Founding study. A tutor helped 3-to-5-year-olds build a block pyramid, taking over the parts the child could not yet do. Origin of the word scaffolding.
numbers: From memory: 30 children aged 3, 4 and 5; one session; tutor functions: recruitment, reduction of degrees of freedom, direction maintenance, marking critical features, frustration control, demonstration.
limits: Not opened; descriptive study with no control group and no effect sizes. Often cited as proof, but it is a case description.
agent_relevance: Gives a function list that maps onto operators (narrow the problem, mark critical features, keep direction).

source: Wood & Middleton (1975) A study of tutoring (contingent instruction)
finding: Mothers who adjusted their help to the child's last success or failure got the best results. Fixed-level help did worse.
numbers: From memory: 12 mother-child pairs, 4-year-olds, a construction puzzle; the contingent rule was to give more help after failure and less after success.
limits: Not opened; very small N; the rule was a coded observation, not a manipulated condition.
agent_relevance: Contingency (step up help after failure, step down after success) is a testable rule for the agent's help level.

source: Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler, Sweller (2003) The expertise reversal effect
finding: Guidance that helps novices can hurt experts, because it duplicates what they already know.
numbers: From memory: series of experiments where worked examples beat problem solving for novices and the order reversed with experience.
limits: Not opened this session; web snippet only confirmed the term. Later reviews note mixed support for some forms.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the lesson scaffold must be skipped when the agent is already competent on that problem type.

source: Pea (2004) The social and technological dimensions of scaffolding
finding: Critique that scaffolding is used loosely and that fading is rarely tested. Proposes that fading and handover be treated as the defining features.
numbers: From memory: conceptual paper, no new effect sizes.
limits: Not opened; recalled from memory.
agent_relevance: Test fading explicitly: measure the agent with the lesson hidden, as Bastani et al. did.

source: Voyager (Wang et al., 2023) ablations: curriculum and skill library
finding: An LLM agent in Minecraft with an automatic curriculum and a growing skill library. Removing the curriculum or the library hurt.
numbers: Random curriculum cut items discovered by 93%. Without the skill library progress plateaued later. Tech tree unlocked 15.3x (wood), 8.5x (stone), 6.4x (iron) faster than baselines; only Voyager reached diamond. 3 runs per level.
limits: Three runs per tech-tree level; one game; GPT-4 needed for code (GPT-3.5 variant was worse).
agent_relevance: Stored skills plus an ordered curriculum act as self-built scaffolds. Order of lessons mattered more than having lessons.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners, ablations
finding: Agent stores trajectories and distils insights. Insights alone and retrieval alone each help; the mix is best, and the better source differs by task.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieve-only: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%; ALFWorld 50% vs 55%. ExpeL matches Reflexion on HotpotQA (40% vs 39%), below it on ALFWorld (54% vs 59%) without repeat attempts.
limits: GPT-3.5/4 era models; success rates are low in absolute terms; four-fold validation.
agent_relevance: Both abstract rules and concrete examples are needed in the lesson memory; the best mix depends on task type.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: insight source and transfer
finding: Insights from a stronger model were better. Insights learned on HotpotQA transferred to FEVER. Hand-written insights helped less than LLM-written ones. Adding reflections to insight writing hurt.
numbers: FEVER success: ReAct 58%, ExpeL transfer without task demos 63%, with demos 65% (table layout garbled in the extracted text). HotpotQA hand-crafted insights above ReAct but below LLM-generated.
limits: Table values read from messy PDF text; check against the paper before quoting.
agent_relevance: Forward transfer of lessons is modest (5 to 7 points) and depends on the quality of the lesson writer.

source: Zhang et al. (2026 v2) ReasoningBank: scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Memory of reasoning strategies distilled from both successes and failures beat raw trajectories and success-only memories.
numbers: WebArena overall success +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 over no-memory for three backbones. Up to 20% relative gain and up to 16% fewer steps. On one backbone table, 49.7 vs Synapse 40.6 vs AWM 44.4.
limits: Success judged by an LLM judge, which may be noisy. Gains vary by site and some domains show small gains.
agent_relevance: Failures kept as preventive lessons add value. Directly relevant to the memory design: store why something failed, not only what worked.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without an outside signal, asking a model to review its own answer lowers accuracy. Gains in earlier papers came from oracle labels.
numbers: With oracle labels GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5; HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0 (table columns partly garbled). Without oracle, accuracy fell on all benchmarks. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time; when it changed, correct-to-wrong exceeded wrong-to-correct.
limits: Table cells reconstructed from PDF text, so pairing may be off. GPT-3.5/4 in 2023; later models may differ.
agent_relevance: A scaffold needs an outside check (tests, verified lesson, other model). Self-review alone is not scaffolding.

source: Burns et al. (2023) Weak-to-strong generalization
finding: Strong models fine-tuned on a weaker model's labels beat the weak supervisor, but only partly. Works on NLP tasks, less on chess and poorly on reward modelling.
numbers: Performance gap recovered above 20% even with very weak supervisors on NLP tasks, often above 50% for the largest students. Chess puzzles: near zero for the weakest supervisors, up to above 40% for small gaps. Poor on ChatGPT reward modelling.
limits: Fine-tuning setup, not in-context scaffolding. Naive finetuning only.
agent_relevance: A weaker guide can lift a stronger learner, but the lift is incomplete and task dependent. Do not assume a lesson from a weak source is safe.

source: Saha, Hase, Bansal (2023) Can language models teach weaker agents?
finding: A teacher LLM giving explanations lifts a weaker student LLM, more with more intervention. Budgeted, personalised help does better than random help.
numbers: Flan-T5-Large 58% to 63% using Flan-T5-XL explanations on StrategyQA. LLaMA-65B teaching LLaMA-7B: about +8% (p=0.01). Expected-utility intervention +7 points at a 20% budget; peak 71% at 40% intervention; accuracy fell 69% to 63% beyond 60% because teacher is imperfect. Personalised teacher peak 72.63%.
limits: Student and teacher are small models; a smaller teacher did not help a larger student (monotone decline).
agent_relevance: Supports contingent help: intervene where the learner is least confident. Over-helping with an imperfect teacher lowers accuracy.

source: Saha, Hase, Bansal (2023) teacher explanations generalise; misleading teacher
finding: Explained examples improved the student on later unexplained items. A misaligned teacher can push the student to chance.
numbers: Future unexplained points: 55% to 61.6% (+6, significant). Misaligned teacher: random-chance accuracy at 60% intervention; non-factual explanations cut accuracy a further 2 points vs benign.
limits: Student prompt contents are in-context demonstrations, not weight updates.
agent_relevance: Lessons carry over to new problems (+6), and bad lessons carry over too. Scaffold content is a trust surface.

source: Dinucu-Jianu, Macina, Daheim, Hakimi, Gurevych, Sachan (2025) From problem-solving to teaching problem-solving
finding: Stock LLMs are tuned to answer and so leak solutions. RL against a simulated student, with a leakage penalty, gives a tutor on the pedagogy-vs-success frontier.
numbers: Student solve-rate gain: Qwen2.5-72B 38.7, DeepSeek-V3 39.3, GPT-4o 33.1, but high leakage; LearnLM 2.0 Flash 4.3, LearnLM 1.5 Pro 1.5, with strong pedagogy. A 7B RL model with penalty weight tuned reaches similar tutoring quality to LearnLM.
limits: Students are simulated by LLMs, not real children. Leak and pedagogy scores come from LLM judges. Per-row leak numbers were unreadable in the extracted table.
agent_relevance: Clear trade-off: more help raises immediate solve rate, more withholding raises pedagogy. The agent's scaffold needs a dial.

source: Scarlatos, Liu, Lee, Baraniuk, Lan (2025) Training LLM-based tutors to improve student learning outcomes in dialogues
finding: Preference-tuning Llama 3.1 8B to raise predicted student correctness while keeping a rubric raised correctness over GPT-4o by 33% in the automatic score.
numbers: Automatic: +33% student-correctness prediction over GPT-4o. Human rating: correctness rank DPO 1.75 vs human tutor 2.12 vs GPT-4o 2.13 (lower is better); rubric DPO 8.55, GPT-4o 8.07, human 7.36 (all p<0.05). Inter-annotator agreement was low (Kendall tau 0.06).
limits: Student is simulated (LLMKT, AUC 0.76 on MathDial). Raters disagree strongly on correctness rank. Rubric scored by GPT-4o, which may favour itself.
agent_relevance: Optimising a learner model's next-step success is possible, but the proxy is noisy; do not trust a single judge.

source: Wei et al. (2026) UCO: multi-turn interactive RL for adaptive teaching
finding: A scaffold reward that targets the student's zone of proximal development improved tutoring over a version without it.
numbers: BigMath ablation: full UCO solve rate 30.2%, leakage 12.9%; without scaffold reward 23.5% and 20.2% leakage; without progress reward 28.6% and 15.6%. Beats 11 baselines of equal scale per authors.
limits: Simulated students; the ZPD is operationalised as reward shaping, not measured in humans.
agent_relevance: Evidence from an ablation that matching difficulty to the learner (not just answering) adds about 7 points of solve rate.

source: Yu, Lee, Feng (2026) STRETCH: self-taught framework with a stretch zone
finding: A model alternates between a Scaffolder that sets tasks at the edge of its ability and a Learner. Frozen or external scaffolders plateaued.
numbers: CraigslistBargain, Qwen2.5-7B: success 0.79 vs R-Zero 0.72 and AZR 0.73; price gap 0.61. Complex OR: execution 58.7%, solving accuracy 55.0% vs StepORLM 57.3% and 52.6%. Mano Complex 63.6% SA vs AZR 60.1%.
limits: Gains are a few points; seeds not checked; authors note STRETCH is not best on every metric. Ablation values are in a figure that was not extracted.
agent_relevance: A self-set difficulty ladder matched to current ability is a usable internal curriculum, small but consistent gain.
